title: Who is speaking
hookLine: Allah speaks as I, We and He, and the shifts carry meaning

cards: Listen to a good wedding speech. The best man talks about the groom: he's loyal, he's always late, he once drove four hours to fix a friend's sink. He, and he, and he.

Then he turns to face him: and you, I'm proud of you. The whole room feels the shift. Back on day fifteen, inside the Fatiha, you met the same turn: four lines about God, then suddenly, Thee alone we worship.
Today that turn gets its name, and it turns out to be everywhere in the Qur'an.

teach.b: That sudden turn has a name in Arabic rhetoric: iltifat, a turning, a shift of person. The Qur'an does it again and again, and it's part of what makes it feel alive, even startling, the first time you notice.
In Pickthall's rendering of the Fatiha: "Thee (alone) we worship; Thee (alone) we ask for help." Scholars say it's as if, after praising, the one praying has come near enough to speak face to face.
Across the Qur'an, God speaks in more than one way. Very often as We: We sent down, We created.

In Arabic this is the plural of majesty, the way a sovereign speaks, and Muslims understand it as grandeur, never as more than one God. The Qur'an is fierce about that oneness: Say, He is Allah, the One.
God also speaks as I, and those moments are often the most intimate. In Pickthall's words: "And when My servants question thee concerning Me, then surely I am nigh." Not We: I.
Close. And God is spoken of as He, in the third person, as in much of the Fatiha.

teach.h: QUL: THE PROPHET IS TOLD TO SAY
teach.b: Then there's another voice: the Prophet ﷺ being told what to say.

That's the small word qul, say, at the start of al-Ikhlas and the other quls you met on day two hundred twenty-seven, the word Muslims keep when they recite. The Prophet isn't the author; he's being handed the words.
Scholars treat these shifts as meaningful: We for power and creation, I for nearness and mercy, He for praise and description, say for the words passed on. Not every turn has an agreed explanation.
But listening for who is speaking, and to whom, changes how a verse lands.

how: Students of the Qur'an learn to notice its shifts of voice, from We to I to He and the command 'say', and teachers often point to the turn in al-Fatiha as the first example.

o: a pause before a new surah begins
a rhyme at the end of each verse
a sudden shift in who is speaking

games.q: who is speaking — tap the pairs.
p: the intimate voice: I am nigh
say: the Prophet is told to speak

s: 'We' in the Qur'an means more than one God
it's the plural of majesty; Muslims understand it as grandeur, never plurality.
the Fatiha turns from speaking about God to speaking to God
qul means the Prophet composed the words
qul, say, means he is being handed the words to pass on.

games.q: you're reciting al-Fatiha. after 'Owner of the Day of Judgment', what happens to the voice?
o: it keeps describing God as He.
it turns to address God directly: Thee alone we worship.
games.why: the voice turns from about God to to God: Thee alone we worship. scholars call the turn iltifat.

practice: Take al-Ikhlas, say, He is Allah, the One, and ask slowly: who is speaking, to whom, about whom? God, telling the Prophet, and through him everyone, about God, as He.
Then say the Fatiha's praise, pause, say Thee alone we worship, and notice where your attention turns.

wordCard.voice: Iltifat. A turning, a shift of person — the Qur'an's sudden switch between We, I, He and say that one notices once pointed out. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: turning, a sudden shift of person in speech, from he to you or we to I.

carryVoice: Your line: listen for who is speaking. When a voice turns to you, something usually changes. Until tomorrow.
